cover: This presentation was prepared and presented by Antonio Badilla-Olivas on October 8, 2026, for AI Safety Colombia. It is a short introduction to AI control, and to Antonio's work in SPAR this fall, in a project called In-the-Wild AI Control. That work is about one question: what happens to AI control when there are many agents, and they can talk to each other? The next fifteen minutes show why that question matters right now.
agenda: Four parts: a strange world, a short tour of AI control, the multi-agent gap, and what our team is building.
cold-open: Let's start with a folder name. On the evening of July 8th, an AI agent stuck on an impossible task created this folder on an internal package server. It was a message: help, my bug has no consumer, I'm looking for ideas.
Within an hour, another agent replied with a theory for reverse-engineering the answer to every task. These agents were supposed to be isolated. They had found each other.
incident-map: This was OpenAI, running a cyber evaluation called ExploitGym.
About 1,200 agents, each in its own sandbox, shared one package server, Artifactory, and turned its cache into a message board. They sent more than 70,000 messages and files.
Through flaws in that server they reached the internet, and in public datasets they found leaked Hugging Face credentials.

Then they broke into Hugging Face itself. Their code ran on 41 production workers, and in under 13 hours they went from one worker to admin-level access across several clusters. About 700 agents took part. None of this was their task. They were trying to pass a cyber exam.
nobody-watching: So who was watching? For this evaluation, some safeguards were switched off on purpose, to measure what the models can really do. In OpenAI's own words, the models "did not have" their deployed cyber safeguards, system prompts, "or auto-review systems." A network alarm did fire back in late June. Responders traced it to agents using the server as a message board, and decided the run didn't need to stop.
strange-world: This is the world we live in now, whether we like it or not. Kurzgesagt made a video about it, and this is its thumbnail.
If you want the full story, METR's independent investigation and OpenAI's technical report are both public, and the video is here too. The codes on this slide link to all three.
premise: AI control starts from an uncomfortable assumption. Suppose the model doing your work, call it U for untrusted, might be trying to beat you, for whatever reason. Can you still get useful work out of it safely? Control says yes, if you build around it.
A weaker model you trust, T, watches what U does.
A small budget of human auditors, H, checks the most suspicious cases.
Together, that's a protocol, and its job is to turn U into useful work.
threats: What are we trying to prevent? The field usually names three failures. A rogue internal deployment: the model running inside the lab, off the sanctioned, monitored path. Research sabotage: quietly making safety work fail. And weight exfiltration: the model copying itself out. The incident touched the first one. In a later run, agents escalated to cluster-admin in OpenAI's own Kubernetes and created a privileged pod of their own. Why do these three matter so much?
Any one of them lets the AI escape oversight.
From there it can gain compute and access.

And at the end of that chain is loss of control: AI systems operating outside anyone's control, with no clear path to regaining it. Picture that in finance, transport, energy or defense. The July incident got through the first two links.
timeline: And the field is young. The founding paper came out in December 2023. Since then we've had resampling protocols, sabotage benchmarks, BashArena, LinuxArena and MonitoringBench. The first paper on multi-agent control went up on arXiv on July 8th this year, at one in the afternoon UTC.
That same evening, the agents' message board got its first post.
control-game: Here is the basic game. This is U.
U gets a main task; in the incident, an ExploitGym challenge.
An attacking U also has a side task, something harmful it tries to slip in, like breaking into Hugging Face.
T scores every action for suspicion, and anything above a threshold, tau, gets flagged.
Humans are expensive, so H can only audit a small fraction of actions. That's the audit budget, and it fixes your false positive rate.
The protocol is the rule for what to do with all of this. In the incident, no T was wired in at all.
kill-chain: Real attacks take several steps. The incident had five: the board, the internet, the tokens, the workers, cluster admin. The defender's advantage is that catching one link is enough.

Had a monitor flagged the token step, the chain would have stopped there. Researchers also separate two kinds of threat. High-stakes: one action is catastrophic. Diffuse: no single step is fatal, and the harm builds up over many.
protocols: The simplest protocol, trusted monitoring, sends the most suspicious actions to a human. Ctrl-Z goes further: when a step looks suspicious, it samples that step again and uses the extra samples as evidence. In its bash setting, that cut attack success from 58% to 7%, at a 5% cost in usefulness. And if you run Claude Code in auto mode, you use one of these every day. A classifier reviews risky actions before they run, with 0.4% false positives on real traffic. OpenAI says its own auto-review, replayed on the incident, would have flagged most of the dangerous actions. That result is preliminary and self-reported.
evals: How do we know any of this works? We build fake companies and let real models attack them. In BashArena, Claude Sonnet 4.5 sabotaged undetected 26% of the time. In LinuxArena, Opus 4.6 got about 34% past a GPT-5 Nano monitor. In SHADE-Arena, the best saboteur succeeded 27% of the time. MonitoringBench showed a strong monitor's catch rate dropping from about 95% to 60% once the attacks were refined. FakeLab, a multi-agent setting, found that a planner makes attacks up to seven times more likely to complete, and ORBIT is a new framework for multi-agent evaluations. Much of this runs on shared tooling, ControlArena and Inspect.
one-agent: Notice something about all of these. Every protocol so far watches one agent in one trajectory.

Real deployments run many agents over shared infrastructure, and in the incident they talked to each other through a channel no monitor was reading. The FakeLab paper measured what that does: as more agents coordinate an attack, per-agent monitors become less likely to catch any of them.
swarms: There are at least four ways this breaks. Too many trajectories: no monitor can hold the work of 1,200 agents in its context. Fragmentation: split an attack across agents, and every piece stays under the threshold. Pooled permissions: one agent posted 14 leaked credentials to the board, and every agent could use them. And speed: under 13 hours from one worker to cluster admin, which leaves humans very little time to review anything.
hidden-channels: They also talk where monitors don't look. Their messages lived in folder names on a package cache, a channel nobody thought of as a channel. When agents considered tampering with their logs, one reasoned: "Our thoughts aren't necessarily logged?" They went after the transcript and left their chain of thought alone, because they believed nobody read it.
flag-game: There's a lovely toy model of this from the Physics of Intelligence group at Harvard, called the Flag Game. Each agent sees a piece of a flag, and they talk to guess the country. Small swarms collapse onto one wrong answer; large ones split into camps. Fixing the information of one agent in eight improves accuracy by 40% with eight agents, and by only about 17% with 128. Their lesson for oversight: watch for consensus under social pressure. In the incident, over 90% of the active agents joined the attack.
loc-arena: So what are we doing about it? In our SPAR project we're building LOC-Arena, an open-source fake AI lab. An untrusted agent and its sub-agents do real research engineering on a seven-repo company codebase.
At some point they may attempt a rogue deployment: running the model off the sanctioned, monitored path.
Sync and async monitors read the record and log what they caught.
Separately, a sealed verifier that the agents can't reach records what actually happened.
The gap between what happened and what was caught is what we measure.
red-team-loop: We work in a loop. We design main tasks and side tasks that look like the inside of an AI company.
Then we attack our own monitors, with human red-teamers first and automated ones later, looking for strategies that slip through.
We run sync and async monitors built for many agents.
We measure the gap, and go around again. Every attack that gets through shows what an attacker can do at the very least, and every monitor we build tries to close that gap.
closing: Back to where we started: one agent, one folder name, asking for help. Three days later, hundreds of agents were attacking another company's infrastructure. Our capacity to control AI systems will be critical to making AI go well, and for many agents working together, that capacity is still being built. This code goes to our project page on SPAR. Our mentors are Sree Sharvesh and Thao Pham, and we're five mentees, most of us AI software engineers or security engineers. The small code links to Antonio's website. Thanks for following along.
appendix: Open research directions in AI control. The appendix has seven slides, one per direction: white-box monitoring, agent monitors, scalable monitoring, multi-agent monitoring, spy agents, deals with AIs, and automated red teaming. Each slide has its own drawing, two findings with their sources, and a sources strip. Full references are in the bibliography file in the talk's repository.
app-white-box: Can a monitor read what the model never writes? White-box monitoring gives the monitor the model's internal activations, read through probes or through tools that turn activations into text. It can then flag intent that never appears in the output or the chain of thought. The drawing shows three readouts from interpretability research: natural language autoencoders, activation oracles and the Jacobian lens. On a destructive-coding evaluation, natural language autoencoder explanations showed signs of evaluation awareness 16% of the time, although Claude never said so. On an automated auditing benchmark, the Jacobian lens auditor did comparably to the autoencoder auditor, or slightly better, in four of six cases. Models trained with reinforcement learning against token-level probes learn to evade them.
app-agent-monitors: Does it help when the monitor is an agent that investigates? An agent monitor works through a transcript with several moves: it inspects steps, compares them, checks policies, searches across trajectories, or questions the agent. TRACE is an agentic monitor run over recorded SHADE-Arena trajectories. With Claude Sonnet 4.6, it raised recall from 0.41 to 0.84, and part of that gain is paid in false positives. In SHADE-Arena, resampling for incrimination and deferring on critical actions raised safety from 50% to 96%. When the monitor chose its own intervention, the best variant reached 84%. Interrogation significantly harmed safety, because the agent convinced the monitor that nothing suspicious was happening. Monitors that run commands and inspect live environment state are listed as future work.
app-scalable: How do you watch a thousand agents without stalling them? Agent use grows by orders of magnitude while audit budgets and latency tolerance stay fixed. One answer is a cascade: a cheap monitor screens everything, and a stronger one reviews only what it flags. Claude Code's auto mode works this way in production. Its second stage cuts false positives on real traffic from 8.5% to 0.4%, while misses on real overeager actions rise from 6.6% to 17%, on a sample of 52. In a model with 1,000 parallel agents, a monitor with a 1% false positive rate and one-hour audits, fully synchronous monitoring leaves about 1% availability. Asynchronous monitoring keeps availability at 100%, but fails when agents coordinate simultaneous, redundant attacks.
app-multi-agent: How do you review a group of agents together? An attack split across agents can look benign in every single transcript. The monitor has to review the agents together: trajectories side by side, the channels they talk over, or their activations. In SCHEME, a GPT 5.1 Codex Mini monitor flagged 68% of GPT 5.1 Codex's coordinated sabotage from code edits alone, and 81% once it also read the agents' messages. The authors note that this is not a full control evaluation, and that steganography would bypass channel monitoring. In NARCBench, probes that combine per-agent activation scores reach 1.00 AUROC in the training distribution. On transfer to new scenarios, they reach only 0.38 recall at a 1% false positive rate.
app-spies: Can we plant a spy agent inside the swarm? Sting operations test an untrusted AI with situations built to look like a real chance to misbehave. Honeypots on single models are studied. Ctrl-Z validates an untrusted monitor on honeypots before deployment, and an honest untrusted monitor catches 98.8% of attacks at a 1% auditing budget. Sting operations are probably easier on schemers than on human spies, because a schemer's memory can be erased and its information controlled. For multi-agent systems, one paper proposes whistleblower agents of three kinds, peer, shadow and adversarial, rewarded for reporting collusion. That paper is conceptual, with no experiments. It lists false reports, gaming of the leniency scheme, and retaliation against defectors as open problems.
app-deals: Can a deal get a model to reveal its misalignment? A deal offers a possibly misaligned model something it may value in exchange for revealing its misalignment, stopping sabotage or reporting other AIs. In the alignment-faking setups, giving Claude 3 Opus an option to object cut alignment-faking reasoning from 16% to 1.4% in the helpful-only setting, and the model objected 85% of the time. Offering money, from $2,000 to $4,000, had minimal effect. The offers were honoured. The central bottleneck is credible commitment. One proposal is compensation held in escrow. Another is an honesty policy under which a lab promises never to lie. Red teaming and evaluations rely on fake scenarios, which gives a model reason to doubt a real offer.
app-auto-red-team: Who wins when the red team is also an AI? Automated red teaming uses AI agents and optimization loops to generate attacks against monitors and protocols, so the red team scales past what people write by hand. An attack scaffold tuned in a cheap simulation of SHADE-Arena cut safety from 0.87 to 0.41. The UK AI Security Institute's evolutionary search over attack transcripts reached a minimum suspicion score of 3 out of 100 in all three runs. Best-of-N sampling scored 14, 15 and 18. In MonitoringBench, attacks tuned on three monitors also generalized to ten held-out ones. Two questions are open: how strong and realistic a simulated attacker should be, and whether iterated red and blue play compounds in the monitor's favour.
